content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Functional vs. Non-Functional Testing in Manual Testing"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding the fundamental differences between functional and non-functional testing is crucial for manual testers. Both are essential pillars of quality assurance, yet they target entirely different aspects of software behavior."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. What is Functional Testing?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Functional testing is a quality assurance process where the system is tested against the functional requirements and specifications. It answers the question: \"Can the user perform specific actions?\" or \"Does the system do what it is supposed to do?\""},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Verifies user interfaces, APIs, database integration, security, and client/server communication."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Focuses heavily on business requirements and user workflows."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Common types include Smoke Testing, Sanity Testing, Regression Testing, and User Acceptance Testing (UAT)."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. What is Non-Functional Testing?"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Non-functional testing evaluates the readiness of a system's non-functional parameters. It addresses how well the system performs rather than specific behaviors. It answers the question: \"How fast does the system load?\" or \"Can it handle thousands of simultaneous users?\""},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Focuses on performance, scalability, usability, reliability, and security."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Measures system behavior under various stress or load conditions."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Common types include Performance Testing, Load Testing, Stress Testing, Usability Testing, and Compatibility Testing."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Key Differences at a Glance"},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Objective: Functional testing validates what the product does; non-functional testing validates how well the product performs."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Execution Priority: Functional testing is typically executed first, followed by non-functional testing."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ease of Manual Execution: Functional testing is straightforward to execute manually. Non-functional testing (like load or stress testing) heavily relies on automation tools, though usability and basic compatibility can be done manually."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Practical Example: E-Commerce Checkout"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider testing an online checkout button. A manual tester applies both methodologies:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"Functional Test Case: Verify that clicking 'Pay Now' with valid credit card details successfully processes the order and redirects to the confirmation page."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"Non-Functional Test Case: Verify that the 'Pay Now' page loads in under 2 seconds even when 5,000 concurrent users are accessing the checkout module."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Both functional and non-functional testing are indispensable. While manual testers spend a significant amount of time validating functional requirements, keeping non-functional parameters like usability and basic responsiveness in mind ensures a comprehensive quality check before product release."}]
